evidence: Skill quality-checks.md #2 asks for sentence variety, contractions and occasional terse fragments, and flags uniform cadence, marketing gloss, perfectly parallel bullets, or a voice shift between instruction.md and notes. instruction.md (9 lines, 5 paragraphs) is written in a first-person-plural firm voice with concrete motivation ('our clients keep emailing documents to whoever answered last', 'a leak is a professional-conduct problem'), varied sentence lengths, short standalone lines (line 7) and contractions (doesn't x2, we'll). The notes keep the same voice: they give situational reasons ('Our internet in court is patchy', 'People fix typos and figures', 'Clients paste all sorts into chat', 'Conflicts come up mid-matter'), switch naturally between we and I ('When I open a matter', 'what I'm doing'), use contractions (can't x4, don't x2, mustn't, isn't, won't, aren't, doesn't, I'm, I've) and include terse lines ('Everyone signs in with `password123`.', 'Dev Anand is walled from M-12 today.'). A grep for gloss/LLM tells (seamless, robust, delve, leverage, ensure, comprehensive, intuitive, streamline, user-friendly, furthermore, moreover, additionally, em/en dashes) found zero hits in all four files. There are no bulleted acceptance lists; the only table is the account roster in walls-and-retention.md lines 49-55, which is reference data, not a stylistic choice. Adversarial read: the notes are dense and precise (for example the timer and hold rules), but they stay in conversational prose with reasons attached, not 'shall/must' spec phrasing. That density is a row 1 or scope concern, not a voice defect. I found no robotic or over-polished passage that would justify a Fail. This row only concerns instruction text, so app or runtime behaviour cannot change it; no runtime evidence is required.
